title: The Last Officer and the Eastern Wall
summary: An isolated imperial remnant falls to a ruler invoking ancient legends, while later alliances and a divided city reshape the surviving institutions.

entries.title: Syren the Officer Called King
entries.body:
Syren signed as provisioning officer while rivals called him king. The distinction shaped succession claims after his death. His surviving accounts reveal effective local government without proving the isolated city remained the center of the empire it invoked.

Later accounts make Syren the Officer Called King the explanation for an entire local change. The surviving record instead places this life among dependencies: an introduction supplied by another household, materials purchased on credit, and testimony given by people with reasons of their own. A biography that removes those dependencies becomes a useful legend and a poor guide to what happened. Descendants inherit evidence and expectations, rather than the ability to repeat an ancestor’s achievement. The practical question is which part of the achievement can be maintained by ordinary people after the celebrated individual is gone.

This belongs to The Last Officer and the Eastern Wall. After the shelf empire dissolved in 349, one cistern city retained its officer, school, and provisioning offices. Neighbors called the officer a king, although his own documents refused the title. In 402 a conquering ruler adopted the name of a legendary ancient sovereign and took the city, promising a restored golden age. Later wars involved southern powers and outside specialists whose aid changed local dependency. An occupation divided the city behind a wall, making its eastern rooms a capital others refused to recognize. Weaving schools carried lessons across successive regimes. Their history preserves practical continuity without accepting every conqueror’s claim that an old name made the present order a reborn original.

In the connected record, [The Eastern Capital Rooms](b036-the-eastern-capital-rooms.md) preserves another part of this history. The terms recorded under [The Successor’s Explicit Scope](b036-the-successor-s-explicit-scope.md) delimit the local obligation; they do not grant a ruler unlimited command over the dead. The unresolved issue in 1248 is concrete: whether reunited city households can share cistern access while untangling obligations authenticated by offices whose legitimacy each successor disputed.

entries.title: The Eastern Capital Rooms
entries.body:
Offices east of the wall issued documents neighbors refused to recognize. Residents still needed birth records, repairs, and water schedules. Their practical dependency complicates histories that describe the sector only through the legitimacy its rulers claimed or were denied.

The site has changed use more than once. Its surviving structures should not be read as a single intact design: one household repairs what another abandoned, and a later occupant can preserve a wall while giving its opening a different purpose. Visitors who search only for the original foundation overlook the people paying for the present roof. Custody depends on continuing access and maintenance, not merely on a persuasive genealogy. Removing an interesting object may erase evidence of a repair that explains why the place remains habitable at all.

entries.title: The Last Imperial School
entries.body:
The school continued teaching after imperial pay ended through household contributions. Conquerors claimed its prestige as evidence of succession. Its records instead document repeated adaptation by teachers and cooks, preserving continuity without automatically transferring every old authority.

The institution’s public account emphasizes its founding purpose, while daily accounts reveal exceptions, unpaid work, and compromises with neighbors. Membership does not imply agreement. A clerk, a patron, and a laborer can defend the same arrangement for incompatible reasons. Its authority is strongest where it provides something people actually need and weakest where it claims that need as proof of permanent jurisdiction. Reform requires deciding who will perform the useful work afterward. Simply abolishing the name may leave the obligation in the hands of less accountable successors.

entries.title: The Ancient Name Conquest
entries.body:
The conqueror took an old royal name before entering the city. Later monuments made resemblance proof of destiny. Supply accounts show unfamiliar troops learning local channels, exposing the ordinary work beneath an advertised return to perfect ancient knowledge.

The event survives through records made for different purposes. A household remembers hunger; a court records jurisdiction; a custodian records the interruption of an observance. Their dates can be reconciled without making their explanations identical. Later commemorations often select a decisive moment because a ceremony needs a beginning and an end. The consequences were less orderly, traveling through marriages, prices, and people who moved away. An honest account follows those consequences far enough to distinguish a temporary outcome from an agreement that still constrains the present.

entries.title: The Officer’s Unroyal Seal
entries.body:
Its plain title remained unchanged through Syren’s isolation. A royal crown was added after his death. Displaying both layers makes later reinterpretation visible, preventing an authentic object from silently proving a title its living owner never used.

Material inspection places limits on the object’s legend. Repairs, wear, and changes in custody can establish that it was used repeatedly without proving every story attached to it. Its value is relational: somebody can authenticate it, somebody needs it for an observance, and somebody may suffer if it is removed. An expensive replacement would not automatically inherit those relations. Custodians therefore record loans and repairs as carefully as ceremonial appearances. A collector who purchases the object but ignores its attached undertaking may own something that cannot safely be taken home.

entries.title: The Name and Task Recited
entries.body:
Officials state a current task beside every inherited title. The custom emerged after repeated renewals brought new fees. It asks whether prestige corresponds to an actual service, without denying that old names can retain meaningful household associations.

The custom is learned through participation rather than a single authoritative text. Households disagree about details while recognizing enough shared actions to cooperate. That flexibility can admit newcomers or allow influential families to redefine the practice in their own favor. Describing it as ancient settles neither possibility. Its practical test is whether a participant can question a demand without losing access to food, water, or witnesses. Local reformers seek finite observances whose costs can be recorded, so that reverence for predecessors does not become an unanswerable demand upon children.

entries.title: The City After the Empire
entries.body:
The history begins with kitchens and schools surviving collapse rather than ending at the throne’s fall. It follows changing office labels. Readers can distinguish cultural and practical continuity from expansive claims made by rulers borrowing that continuity for succession.

Copies disagree in ways that matter. A shortened phrase can remove a condition, and a copied date can imply that a later amendment belonged to the original undertaking. Dry writing preserves evidence but cannot make an oath binding by itself. Readers must distinguish a record of consent from a writer’s assertion that consent occurred. Marginal notes are sometimes the only surviving testimony of people excluded from the formal version. Establishing a trustworthy reading therefore depends on comparing custody, material, and ordinary expenses, as well as elegant arguments about wording.

entries.title: The Wall Cistern Blind Fish
entries.body:
Small pale fish inhabit interconnected drains crossing the former wall. Officials sealed channels to secure division and damaged water quality on both sides. Reopening selected passages restored habitat and practical cooperation before political reunion was agreed.

Reports describe a living creature before they describe a supernatural emblem. It needs food, shelter, and a place to breed, and it reacts to disturbances that witnesses may misunderstand. A keeper who recognizes those needs can often prevent the encounter later remembered as a curse. The animal cannot be made into an obedient instrument of ancestral power. Where an undertaking changes its habitat, the effect is indirect and costly to other inhabitants. Stories that treat its behavior as a moral verdict obscure both ordinary suffering and the human decisions that altered the site.

entries.title: The Weavers’ Wall Passage
entries.body:
Weaving teachers crossed through a narrow work permit route carrying samples and lesson leaves. Guards disputed their authority but needed textiles. The passage preserved knowledge through constrained cooperation rather than an uninterrupted freedom later commemorations sometimes imagine.

A route is an agreement between people maintaining its difficult portions, as much as a line across terrain. Tolls buy repairs only when their recipients are accountable for the work. A passage described as open may still be unusable for children, loaded animals, or travelers without an accepted witness. Seasonal detours preserve movement while distributing its costs to other households. Pilots and guides keep alternative accounts of distance because time, provisions, and exposure matter more than ceremonial measures. Closing one stretch can therefore revise obligations far beyond its immediate neighborhood.

entries.title: The Successor’s Explicit Scope
entries.body:
A successor must identify which undertakings an inherited office can actually authenticate. Titles alone do not confer unlimited jurisdiction. The rule makes continued service possible while exposing the broader authority repeatedly claimed through legendary names.

The rule’s force depends on a stated scope. It governs named acts and claimants, rather than every future disagreement that resembles its original case. Courts have nevertheless tried to extend it, usually when a narrow precedent would benefit a powerful applicant. Opponents do not have to deny ancestor law to challenge that extension. They can ask which promise was actually made, who witnessed it, and whether the required observance remains possible. The difference between a valid undertaking and a convenient assertion of authority is central to the current dispute.

entries.title: The First Wall Gate Closure
entries.body:
Gate closure separated relatives and workers within one afternoon. Officials provided no alternate repair route. Plumbing failures followed quickly, illustrating how political separation depended on material systems that remained connected beneath the intended boundary.

The event survives through records made for different purposes. A household remembers hunger; a court records jurisdiction; a custodian records the interruption of an observance. Their dates can be reconciled without making their explanations identical. Later commemorations often select a decisive moment because a ceremony needs a beginning and an end. The consequences were less orderly, traveling through marriages, prices, and people who moved away. An honest account follows those consequences far enough to distinguish a temporary outcome from an agreement that still constrains the present.

entries.title: The Legendary King’s New Brick
entries.body:
A conquest brick bears an old name in a new script. Its maker marks identify contemporary workers. The object displays deliberate revival rather than literal continuity, making the political use of ancient prestige inspectable.

Material inspection places limits on the object’s legend. Repairs, wear, and changes in custody can establish that it was used repeatedly without proving every story attached to it. Its value is relational: somebody can authenticate it, somebody needs it for an observance, and somebody may suffer if it is removed. An expensive replacement would not automatically inherit those relations. Custodians therefore record loans and repairs as carefully as ceremonial appearances. A collector who purchases the object but ignores its attached undertaking may own something that cannot safely be taken home.

entries.title: The Shared Calendar Meal
entries.body:
Households explain both sector dates before recording a new agreement. The custom prevents mismatched anniversaries becoming accusations of broken observance. Reconciliation begins through usable conversions rather than requiring one community’s remembered time to be erased.

The custom is learned through participation rather than a single authoritative text. Households disagree about details while recognizing enough shared actions to cooperate. That flexibility can admit newcomers or allow influential families to redefine the practice in their own favor. Describing it as ancient settles neither possibility. Its practical test is whether a participant can question a demand without losing access to food, water, or witnesses. Local reformers seek finite observances whose costs can be recorded, so that reverence for predecessors does not become an unanswerable demand upon children.

entries.title: The Capitals Not Recognized
entries.body:
This register records documents useful locally despite denied external authority. It does not endorse every regime issuing them. It shows why rejecting political legitimacy and denying a resident’s ordinary recorded life are different acts with different costs.

Copies disagree in ways that matter. A shortened phrase can remove a condition, and a copied date can imply that a later amendment belonged to the original undertaking. Dry writing preserves evidence but cannot make an oath binding by itself. Readers must distinguish a record of consent from a writer’s assertion that consent occurred. Marginal notes are sometimes the only surviving testimony of people excluded from the formal version. Establishing a trustworthy reading therefore depends on comparing custody, material, and ordinary expenses, as well as elegant arguments about wording.

entries.title: The Wall’s Unended Pressure
entries.body:
A sealed channel presses water against the old division after reunion. Masonry explains the blockage, but an unfinished access pledge complicates removal. Keepers seek consent and repairs together, addressing both material obstruction and the finite obligation attached to it.

Witnesses distinguish an observed effect from their explanation for it. Repetition under comparable conditions is valuable evidence; a striking story told after its alleged cause becomes famous is weaker evidence. Masons, gardeners, and boat crews often recognize patterns an interpreter overlooks. Their explanation may reduce the immediate danger without settling whether an undertaking contributed to it. The basin has no institution capable of issuing a final answer for every manifestation. Communities record the conditions under which the effect occurs, then negotiate a response whose costs they can actually sustain.

entries.title: Calendar Conversion Teaching
entries.body:
Teachers compare dated household transactions to reconcile rival calendars. Errors affect inheritance and fees. The craft is slow and ordinary, yet essential to making reunion real for people whose lives crossed regimes with incompatible official measures of time.

The trade depends upon tools, training, reliable materials, and people who perform work its public account barely mentions. A skilled craftsperson can improve a process, yet every batch still requires hands and a season of available materials. Output remains bounded by fuel, animals, weather, and the hands available to repair equipment. Prices carry the history of these constraints into households far from the workshop. A commercial undertaking that survives its maker can preserve useful cooperation or prevent successors from adapting to changed conditions. The present negotiation concerns how to retain knowledge while releasing an obligation nobody can now perform.

entries.title: The Officer’s Surviving Claims
entries.body:
Descendants seek rights under an imperial office later courts deny. Current households depend on some of its valid undertakings. The hearing separates those finite commitments from the impossible demand to revive an entire vanished jurisdiction.

The dispute contains more than two positions. People with the same formal entitlement may face different practical costs, while opponents can depend upon the same canal, kitchen, or crossing. A complete settlement must describe an executable change rather than award a satisfying phrase to one side. Evidence about a past wrong remains necessary even when compensation cannot restore the original arrangement. Local negotiators separate immediate maintenance from the final assessment of responsibility. This allows a place to remain usable while its inhabitants continue an argument they have good reason not to abandon.
